cards.explanation: The answer is False. The man asks God to "answer me quickly when I call." He's in a day of distress, and he asks the LORD not to hide His face from him. Nobody in that spot says, "No rush, whenever you get to it."

The answer is that his life is slipping away, friends. Smoke doesn't stay put. You try to grab it and your hand comes back empty. He says his days "…vanish like smoke…" and I think he's saying his life feels like it's disappearing on him.
The answer is eat, bakers. The man says, "I even forget to eat my bread." His heart is afflicted and withered like grass, he says. I think the man is carrying something heavy, and the verse shows it.

The answer is that he feels all alone, friends. He says he's like a desert owl, like an owl among the ruins, and like a lone bird on a housetop. I think those pictures say he feels all alone. He also says he lies awake, and I bet that's a lonely stretch for him.
The answer is True, friends. He says, "All day long my enemies taunt me…" All day, not just once in a while. It's a long stretch to carry that on top of feeling alone.

The answer is God's indignation and wrath. That's what the man says. He eats ashes like bread and mixes his drink with tears "…because of Your indignation and wrath…" He's talking straight to the LORD when he says it. It's a heavy verse, so I'll just let it sit there.

The answer is late in the day, friends. When the sun gets low, shadows stretch out long, and that tells you the day is winding down. I think that's the feeling he's after. His days are like lengthening shadows and he withers away like grass.

The answer is that the LORD sits enthroned forever. That's the turn. The man says, "But You, O LORD, sit enthroned forever…" His own days are fading like shadows, and he looks up at the One whose throne doesn't fade. That's a lot of comfort packed into a few words.
The answer is False, friends. The man tells the LORD, "…it is time to show her favor…" He also says, "…the appointed time has come." That's the opposite of saying her time hasn't come yet.

The answer is True, friends. The man says, "So the nations will fear the name of the LORD, and all the kings of the earth will fear Your glory." Nations and kings, the whole lineup. It's a big picture.

The answer is rebuild, friends. Just before that, the man says God's servants delight in her stones and take pity on her dust. Then he says, "For the LORD will rebuild Zion…" The LORD is the one who builds her back up.

The answer is False, friends. Verse 17 says, "He will turn toward the prayer of the destitute; He will not despise their prayer." The LORD turns toward those prayers, and He doesn't despise them. That comes right after the man says the LORD has appeared in His glory.

The answer is so future people can praise the LORD. The man says, "Let this be written for the generation to come, so that a people not yet created may praise the LORD." He's asking for it to be written for people who haven't even been born yet. I think that's a generous thing to do.

The answer is a prisoner's groaning, friends. The text says the LORD gazed out from heaven to earth "…to hear a prisoner’s groaning…" He looked down from the heights of His sanctuary to do it. God looked down to listen to someone who was groaning, and that's the whole picture.

The answer is release, friends. The LORD looked down "…to hear a prisoner’s groaning, to release those condemned to death…" The verse puts hearing the groaning and releasing those condemned to death side by side, and I think that's beautiful.

The answer is that he asks God not to take him in the middle of his days, friends. He says, "O my God, do not take me in the midst of my days!" His strength is broken and his days are cut short, and he asks God for more time. I think you can hear how much he means it.

The answer is that they will perish and wear out. The man says, "They will perish, but You remain; they will all wear out like a garment." Even the heavens and the earth wear out like old clothes. And then comes the but: God remains.

The answer is False, friends. The prayer ends with, "The children of Your servants will dwell securely, and their descendants will be established before You." After all those hard verses, it lands on safe and steady. The man says it just after saying God remains the same and His years will never end.
